newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds end stronger as Fed holds rates.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds end stronger as Fed holds rates.

text.p: Canadian bonds and T-bills closed stronger on Tuesday and outperformed U.S. Treasuries, as the Canadian dollar rallied on a decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve not to raise interest rates, analysts said.

"With the Fed not doing anything there was an immediate reaction by the Canadian dollar," said Barry Allan, vice-president of global fixed income with Altamira Investment Services. "That immediately translated into people buying short Canada, the short end of the Canadian curve," he said.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.30 to C$111.75 to yield 7.011 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond rose 8/32 to yield of 6.90 percent. The spread between the bonds narrowed to 11 basis points from 14 basis points at the close of trading on Friday.

The Fed's rate-setting Open Market Committee concluded its meeting today without raising U.S. rates. Financial markets had been evenly divided on the possibility that the Fed would hike rates and rallied after the decision was announced.

"The best performance has probably been in the very short end, the two year and bill area, which is no surprise. I think there's some unwinding of flattening trades happening here," said one bond trader with a bank-owned brokerage.

The Canadian dollar rallied sharply following the news from the Fed, surging past C$1.37 (US$0.7299). There had been some concern that a hike in U.S. rates would put downward pressure on the currency, as the Bank of Canada was not seen immediately matching a Fed tightening.

"The pressure is off the Canadian dollar, and the Canadian dollar is probably going to rally from here, so you want to own the short end of the Canadian curve," said Altamira's Allan. "I think everybody is trying to buy the short end of Canada against the U.S."
In ratings news, Dominion Bond Rating Service on Tuesday said it upgraded its debt ratings for the Canadian province of Saskatchewan to reflect its improving fiscal situation.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.41 to C$103.76 to yield 6.464 percent. The U.S. 10-year bond rose 9/32 to yield 6.67 percent.
The negative spread between the two bonds widened to 21 basis points from 18 basis points at Friday's close.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 3.02 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.22 percent.
